profiles.summary: A practical study of how fictional people become psychologically legible rather than merely accumulating quirks. Corbett treats character construction as an inquiry into pressures, decisions, experience and behavior; the book offers writers exercises and examples rather than a universal scientific explanation of personality.
profiles.author_and_work_background: David Corbett published The Art of Character: Creating Memorable Characters for Fiction, Film, and TV with Penguin Books in 2013. His experience in investigative work and crime fiction informs its close attention to lived contradiction, social environment and active observation. Its publisher and college-library catalogs confirm the publication, not the efficacy of every technique.
profiles.before_reading: Try a character you know from a favorite novel and separate what the narrator tells you from what the person actually does. Keep one page for contradictions: loyalties that collide with appetites, strengths that become liabilities and choices that reveal desire under pressure. Treat each exercise as a craft experiment, not a clinical diagnostic.
profiles.literary_approach: The guide builds characterization through behavioral specificity, inward conflict and the pressures of relationships. It is most useful when applied to a difficult scene rather than read as a checklist of personality adjectives. The idea of credibility is a readerly judgment: careful examples help, but no one writing system guarantees a compelling result.
profiles.context: Corbett writes within a contemporary professional craft-book tradition that borrows examples from literature and screen storytelling. His approach can be set beside Lisa Cron’s causal model and John Truby’s design framework: the three often agree that action is revelatory, while prioritizing different engines for that action. Their published advice is not controlled experimental evidence.

themes.label: Contradiction
themes.discussion: A believable person can want incompatible goods at the same moment.

themes.label: Behavioral evidence
themes.discussion: The reader learns character from choice under constraint.

themes.label: Social formation
themes.discussion: Family, work, culture and power shape the options that appear available.

profiles.personal_fit: Especially helpful when developing the intricate motivations and changing alliances of an emotionally driven novel.
profiles.possible_mismatch: Its abundance of exercises can feel prescriptive if the reader wants literary criticism rather than a writing workbook.

notes: Discussion of violence, trauma and difficult human behavior through writing examples; exact contents vary by printing.

reading_questions: Which of your favorite characters has a revealing discrepancy between stated belief and action?
How would a mundane obligation expose the same character more effectively than a dramatic confession?
What would change if this character were deprived of the social role that protects them?
When does empathy for a fictional person become an excuse for their conduct?
discussion_questions: Which exercise produces an unexpectedly specific scene rather than a generic backstory?
Where could you deliberately resist Corbett’s method?

profiles.author: Leo Tolstoy

series.name: Standalone
series.sequence_status: Informational connections only. All ordinary books can be manually shuffled or reordered by the reader.

profiles.summary: The respectable life of a well-placed magistrate is unsettled by serious illness and the prospect of death. Tolstoy follows the gap between a socially successful biography and an inner life that cannot find comfort in official rituals, asking what a person has mistaken for living well.
profiles.author_and_work_background: Tolstoy first published The Death of Ivan Ilyich in Russian in 1886, decades after the early novels and in the period of his more explicit moral writing. The University of Minnesota’s open educational edition presents an English text and historical context. Named later English examples include the Maudes and Richard Pevear with Larissa Volokhonsky; their word choices are not interchangeable.
profiles.before_reading: Notice how swiftly other people translate mortality into inconvenience or career opportunity. This is a short work that rewards deliberate stops after each social encounter: ask which language feels rehearsed and which language allows genuine suffering to be acknowledged. Keep the ending unspoiled and watch for recurring physical and spatial imagery.
profiles.literary_approach: Tolstoy uses close third-person narration, condensed chronology and abrasive social observation. The stark ordinariness of furniture, workplace etiquette and medical consultations keeps ethical questions anchored in material experience. His irony exposes the difference between external propriety and the vulnerability that society prefers not to see.
profiles.context: The novella is often situated within Tolstoy’s later moral and religious preoccupations, but its emotional force does not require sharing his conclusions. Translation alters levels of formality, the rhythm of repetitive phrases and the treatment of Russian names. Compare a specific paragraph in a Maude text and a Pevear/Volokhonsky edition before assigning either an overall superiority.

themes.label: The performance of success
themes.discussion: Social approval can conceal rather than answer existential questions.

themes.label: Embodied fear
themes.discussion: Pain resists the tidy narrative people tell about a respectable life.

themes.label: Care and honesty
themes.discussion: The smallest acts of attention can compete with institutional politeness.

profiles.personal_fit: A concentrated classic for a reader who values intense interior writing and moral complexity; pairs naturally with your yearlong Tolstoy read.
profiles.possible_mismatch: The direct focus on terminal illness and isolation may be especially heavy during a time of loss or anxiety.

notes: Terminal illness, fear of death, emotional neglect, intense suffering and death.

reading_questions: What does the opening teach about the social cost of death before introducing Ivan’s experience?
Which object or room detail changes in emotional significance during the narrative?
How do characters distinguish politeness from kindness?
What words would you compare across two translations, and why?
discussion_questions: Where does narrative irony sharpen compassion rather than ridicule?
How does the novella complicate your reading of Tolstoy in War and Peace?

series.sequence_status: Informational connections only. All ordinary books can be manually shuffled or reordered by the reader.

profiles.summary: In the later Earthsea world, a humble sorcerer’s recurring dreams and the unease surrounding the boundary between life and death bring several longstanding questions into conversation. The novel gathers different voices rather than simply arranging an escalating magical contest, making the experience of listening itself part of its action.
profiles.author_and_work_background: Ursula K. Le Guin’s own bibliography dates The Other Wind to 2001 and identifies Harcourt as its original publisher. Her Earthsea pages explain that the story “Dragonfly” in Tales from Earthsea provides an important bridge after Tehanu. Some publishers call The Other Wind a fifth Earthsea novel, while shelving systems list a sixth book when including the story collection: edition labels are not a reliable reading-order authority.
profiles.before_reading: Read this after Tehanu and the bridging tale if you want to retain the intended sequence, but Rosewood will not prevent you from choosing another order. Avoid looking up summaries that explain the larger series conclusion. Instead note whose perspectives carry authority in the early chapters, and how silence and memory complicate apparent certainties.
profiles.literary_approach: The prose relies on patient dialogue, changes in scale and the revision of apparently settled cultural myths. Le Guin frequently makes the powerful hear people they have dismissed; the movement toward collective understanding is an artistic method rather than a simple replacement for action. Its quietly radical emphasis on relationship is central to its craft.
profiles.context: The official author bibliography and Earthsea introduction support the 2001 date and the cycle’s structure. The book belongs to Le Guin’s long revisiting of gender, power, naming and mortality, with important changes of emphasis since the 1968 first novel. Comparisons with earlier books are illuminating, but can spoil characters and revelations for new readers.

themes.label: Boundaries
themes.discussion: Worldbuilding rules can encode moral assumptions that need scrutiny.

themes.label: Many kinds of authority
themes.discussion: Formal power competes with lived experience and neglected testimony.

themes.label: Memory and change
themes.discussion: A series can interrogate its own foundations without discarding its history.

profiles.personal_fit: For a reader drawn to layered fantasy, beautiful spare writing and ethical revision of familiar mythology.
profiles.possible_mismatch: Its force depends partly on earlier Earthsea books and deliberate dialogue; it is not primarily a brisk action adventure.

notes: Mortality, dream distress, grief and supernatural threats; late-series revelations may be upsetting.

reading_questions: How does the opening give dignity to a person with limited formal power?
When is an inherited account of the world presented as incomplete rather than false?
Which conversations change how the reader understands authority?
What earlier Earthsea motif takes on a different moral weight?
discussion_questions: How does Le Guin make restraint produce narrative intensity?
Would the same ending work without the cycle’s prior books?

profiles.verification_scope: Individually scoped public bibliographic claims checked through work-specific sources on 2026-11-20. profiles.genre_and_form: Russian short fiction collection; exact table of contents edition-dependent

series.name: Standalone collection
series.sequence_status: Informational connections only. All ordinary books can be manually shuffled or reordered by the reader.

profiles.summary: A minor clerk invests his hopes in the material dignity of a new coat, only to discover how fragile social recognition can be. In the best-known story by Nikolai Gogol, bureaucratic comedy rubs against pathos and the uncanny; the surrounding stories in a collection can broaden the reader’s sense of his satire.
profiles.author_and_work_background: Gogol’s The Overcoat appeared in Russian in 1842. Unlike a single original novel, The Overcoat and Other Stories names more than one English collection, with different translators and contents. Princeton’s Shakespeare and Company project documents a 1923 collection translated by Constance Garnett; Norton offers a separately assembled David Magarshack collection, while Penguin’s Ronald Wilks appears in another selected-stories volume. Never merge these tables of contents.
profiles.before_reading: Choose which actual collection you will read before importing a page count or tracking individual stories. Keep a list of which tales are included and their English/Russian titles, since different editors translate and group them differently. In the title story, notice how quickly ordinary narration can become outrageously disproportionate.
profiles.literary_approach: Gogol builds satire through repetition, grotesque physical detail, intrusive narrative commentary and unstable shifts between earnest sympathy and absurd laughter. The narrator sometimes appears to lose control of a minor observation; that excess invites a reader to ask whether the fictional society has itself lost any sense of scale.
profiles.context: The Russian work is not interchangeable with every English volume carrying the phrase “other stories.” A Garnett collection from 1923, a Magarshack selection and Ronald Wilks’s selected stories are different publication objects, even when they overlap on the famous text. Compare one passage’s comic register across translations and track who seems to be the object of the joke.

themes.label: Bureaucratic invisibility
themes.discussion: Institutional rank may be mistaken for a measure of personhood.

themes.label: Objects and dignity
themes.discussion: Material goods can hold meanings far beyond their price.

themes.label: Comic instability
themes.discussion: A funny narrative voice can expose as well as reproduce cruelty.

profiles.personal_fit: An excellent introduction to Russian literary satire, with the absurd, psychologically acute writing that connects to Dostoevsky.
profiles.possible_mismatch: If you want one unambiguous novel to count, a collection with edition-dependent contents needs clearer ownership and progress choices.

notes: Humiliation, economic hardship, theft, frightening or uncanny images and social cruelty; story collection contents vary.

reading_questions: When does the narrator laugh with a character rather than at him?
How are officials granted or denied individual faces?
What does the coat represent to its owner that observers fail to see?
How does a second translator handle the most excessive sentence?
discussion_questions: Why might a sudden supernatural turn strengthen social criticism?
Which story would you pair with Notes from Underground and why?

profiles.author: Lisa Cron
profiles.verification_scope: Individually scoped public bibliographic claims checked through work-specific sources on 2026-11-20. series.sequence_status: Informational connections only. All ordinary books can be manually shuffled or reordered by the reader.

profiles.summary: Lisa Cron argues that compelling narrative derives from the character’s internal story: an inherited understanding of the world is challenged by the consequences of choice. The book guides writers from a premise and misbelief toward causally linked scenes, framing the process as a way to avoid drafting without an emotional through-line.
profiles.author_and_work_background: Story Genius was published in 2016 by Ten Speed Press and follows Cron’s earlier Wired for Story. The official publisher describes a scene-by-scene blueprint and invokes brain science to justify a character-driven method. That marketing language should not be confused with independent proof that this writing system is neurologically privileged or universally more effective.
profiles.before_reading: Take a single scene from an existing draft, then write down the belief the viewpoint character brings into it. Identify what external event puts pressure on that belief, what choice the character makes and which consequence will shape the following scene. If the model feels forced, record that resistance rather than rewriting a story to satisfy a workbook.
profiles.literary_approach: Cron’s method emphasizes a through-line of expectation, disconfirmation and consequential response. In practice it is a tool for asking why the reader should care about an event, not a prohibition on exploratory or literary plotting. Try its diagnostic questions on a short story before applying a whole blueprint to a novel.
profiles.context: The 2016 publisher and library records establish a practical professional craft book. Neither its title nor its publisher copy demonstrates causation between brain processes and a universal story structure. A useful comparison is to distinguish the testable claim “readers respond to causal coherence” from the stronger and contestable sales claim that one method guarantees reader immersion.

themes.label: Internal causality
themes.discussion: Why a choice matters depends on what the character believes.

themes.label: Scene consequences
themes.discussion: Actions reshape what is possible in the next moment.

themes.label: Method versus mystery
themes.discussion: A blueprint can illuminate a work but may not capture its best surprises.

profiles.personal_fit: A potentially strong workbook for emotionally complex fiction with specific relationships and sustained inner change.
profiles.possible_mismatch: The brain-science rhetoric may overpromise; readers who enjoy ambiguous or associative fiction may resist rigid causality.

notes: Writing exercises may evoke difficult memories or personal emotional material; no clinical treatment advice is supplied.

Can a compelling scene occur without a dramatic revelation?
Which exercise makes a character more complex rather than easier to explain?

profiles.summary: Cohen the Barbarian and his elderly companions remain committed to an old-fashioned idea of heroic adventure, even as the world moves on without them. The Last Hero turns that stubborn legend into a visually elaborate Discworld fable about mortality, fame and the unexpected consequences of a spectacular gesture.
profiles.author_and_work_background: The Last Hero appeared in 2001 as an illustrated Terry Pratchett Discworld fable, with artwork by Paul Kidby. Original Gollancz and HarperCollins listings identify the illustrated format; later Gollancz editions advertise new cover designs but retain Kidby illustrations. Edition size and layout should therefore be verified rather than borrowing the page count of an earlier hardcover.
profiles.before_reading: Pay attention to images as part of the reading experience. The fable uses familiar Discworld figures, but the illustrations have their own timing and comic emphasis; skimming only the words loses part of its form. The app displays informational series relationships without enforcing a particular order, so choose your own placement.
profiles.literary_approach: Pratchett compresses epic-quest rhetoric into aging bodies, practical concerns and elaborate jokes. Kidby’s images function as narrative collaborators, contrasting heroic tableau with comic human limits. A reader can track how an apparently ridiculous journey forces serious questions without losing the tone of a satire.
profiles.context: The illustrated book is not just a standard prose novel with a detachable cover. Changes between a 2001 illustrated hardcover and subsequent paperback designs may change typography, physical scale and browsing experience. Pratchett’s gentle irreverence about heroism is not the same as dismissing the need for courage.

themes.label: Legacy
themes.discussion: Who decides which achievements survive as a story?

themes.label: Old age and adventure
themes.discussion: Fantasy heroism looks different when a hero’s body changes.

themes.label: Art and text
themes.discussion: Images can provide a second voice of comic and emotional interpretation.

profiles.personal_fit: For Discworld readers who like genre-aware humor, striking illustrations and unexpectedly tender thoughts about aging.
profiles.possible_mismatch: Less suitable for text-only reading experiences that omit or shrink the illustrations; recurring character context enriches some jokes.

notes: Comic peril, weapons, age-related decline, death references and fantasy conflict.

profiles.title: The Social Contract
profiles.author: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
profiles.verification_scope: Individually scoped public bibliographic claims checked through work-specific sources on 2026-11-20. Interpretive prose is original editorial analysis, not a verified complete reading; no owned-ISBN, cover, exact translation, physical edition, page total, audiobook length or exhaustive content-warning certification.

publication.basis: Initial work or original-language story publication (when known), not the date or page count of an owned edition; editions and English collections vary.

series.name: Standalone
series.sequence_status: Informational connections only. All ordinary books can be manually shuffled or reordered by the reader.

profiles.summary: Rousseau asks on what grounds political authority can be legitimate without reducing citizens to subjects of another person’s arbitrary will. His answer centers on collective sovereignty and the general will, but the conditions under which citizens could genuinely share such a will create deep interpretive and political difficulties.
profiles.author_and_work_background: Du contrat social, ou Principes du droit politique appeared in 1762. Jean-Jacques Rousseau distinguished the sovereign people as lawmaking body from the government that administers law, a distinction embedded in his controversial account of freedom. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy records competing interpretations and objections; Cambridge offers a named Victor Gourevitch English translation and associated political writings.
profiles.before_reading: Build a glossary distinguishing “general will,” “will of all,” sovereignty, government, freedom and civil religion. Resist importing contemporary party-politics meanings into 1762 language. Treat the text’s claims about what a legitimate community requires as a philosophical argument, not as a universally accepted description of modern democracy.
profiles.literary_approach: The work proceeds by condensed propositions, paradoxes and a chain of conceptual distinctions. Rousseau’s argument gains sharpness from treating freedom as compatible with law only under demanding conditions. A close reader should test whether apparent solutions actually preserve the individual agency the opening insists must be protected.
profiles.context: Rousseau’s democratic rhetoric has inspired emancipatory readings, but critics also question exclusion, the pressure exerted by collective will and the notorious idea of being “forced to be free.” Stanford’s scholarly overview treats these as real interpretive tensions. Modern assemblies, representation and pluralism cannot simply be read back into his idealized model.

themes.label: Legitimacy
themes.discussion: Force alone does not explain why power should have authority.

themes.label: Collective freedom
themes.discussion: A shared law may protect agency or suppress dissent, depending on its structure.

themes.label: The missing citizen
themes.discussion: Any ideal of universal participation must be tested against exclusions.

profiles.personal_fit: Useful alongside Kant, Mill, de Beauvoir and the classics of moral and political philosophy in your required reading.
profiles.possible_mismatch: Compressed arguments and historical assumptions demand slow attention; the ideas are neither straightforward slogans nor settled policy advice.

notes: Discussion of coercion, civic exclusion, slavery and religion in an eighteenth-century political context.

reading_questions: Why is consent insufficient if the sovereign can later ignore citizens?
When might an apparently universal law protect an unequal status quo?
What is the distinction between a general will and a majority preference?
Does the argument require a society that is unrealistically homogeneous?
discussion_questions: What is gained and lost by rejecting political representation?
Where might Mill directly challenge Rousseau?

profiles.genre_and_form: Epic military fantasy; first Poppy War trilogy book

series.name: The Poppy War trilogy
series.sequence_status: Informational connections only. All ordinary books can be manually shuffled or reordered by the reader.

profiles.summary: Rin, a poor war orphan, wins entrance to an elite military academy and confronts social hierarchy, brutal training and a form of power that threatens to consume the people who wield it. What begins with academic ambition broadens into a wartime story that insists on the human costs of imperial conflict.
profiles.author_and_work_background: R. F. Kuang’s debut The Poppy War was released in 2018 by Harper Voyager. Publishers Weekly reviewed its blend of military fantasy, training narratives and Asian historical influences. Kuang’s own Goodreads author note explicitly discusses the Second Sino-Japanese War and the Nanjing Massacre as inspirations; this authorial analogy must not be treated as a literal one-to-one history or historical document.
profiles.before_reading: Do not approach this as a comforting magic-school fantasy. The tonal progression includes extremely graphic wartime atrocities and dehumanization. Read the introduction as a challenge to meritocratic escape narratives: Rin’s ability opens doors, but does not dissolve the class structures and violence around her.
profiles.literary_approach: Kuang combines recognizable coming-of-age beats with escalating military stakes, compressing academic competition into geopolitical conflict. The novel shifts a reader’s expectations about mastery and victory: dazzling power is repeatedly measured against its bodily and social price. Its use of historical echoes asks for research and ethical care without collapsing fiction into fact.
profiles.context: The historical analogies to Chinese twentieth-century war are author-declared inspirations, not independent evidence about any historical incident. Claims about particular real events should be checked in historical scholarship outside the novel. The trilogy’s later volumes are deliberately not summarized here, preserving major character and world spoilers.

themes.label: Power and cost
themes.discussion: A capacity for destruction is not the same as wise agency.

themes.label: Education and belonging
themes.discussion: Institutional merit may coexist with exclusion and humiliation.

themes.label: History through fantasy
themes.discussion: Analogies can illuminate atrocity while risking simplification.

profiles.personal_fit: A powerful choice for readers of morally difficult epic fantasy who want politics, ambitious character arcs and high emotional stakes.
profiles.possible_mismatch: Substantially darker than its opening training-school structure suggests; avoid if graphic wartime violence is unwelcome.

notes: Extremely graphic sexual violence and mass atrocities, genocide parallels, torture, war, addiction, self-harm and death; non-exhaustive.

When is determination written as virtue and when as danger?
What does a magical power change about responsibility?
How does the novel revise the reader’s initial genre expectations?
discussion_questions: Where does a historical analogy educate, and where could it mislead?
Which scene changes your understanding of the cost of victory?

profiles.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
profiles.verification_scope: Individually scoped public bibliographic claims checked through work-specific sources on 2026-11-20. profiles.genre_and_form: Russian psychological novella; first-person gambling narrative

series.name: Standalone
series.sequence_status: Informational connections only. All ordinary books can be manually shuffled or reordered by the reader.

profiles.summary: In a fictional European casino town, a young tutor becomes entangled with a volatile household, romantic expectation and roulette. Dostoevsky’s first-person narrator explains his behavior with insistent cleverness while repeatedly demonstrating that understanding a compulsion does not necessarily loosen its grip.
profiles.author_and_work_background: The Gambler first appeared in 1866. The Oxford World’s Classics combined edition Notes from the Underground and The Gambler credits translator Jane Kentish and provides an introduction by Malcolm Jones. Ronald Meyer’s translator bibliography also describes Dostoevsky’s compressed dictation under financial pressure. Earlier Hugh Aplin and other translations represent different choices, not a single standardized English text.
profiles.before_reading: Listen for the narrator’s changing explanations of a lost bet: confidence, inevitability, secret competence and the need for one more attempt. Mark how money and romantic recognition become entangled, and compare the emotional urgency with Notes from Underground. The narrator’s position is not a reliable guide to the motives of everyone around him.
profiles.literary_approach: The breathless first-person narration repeatedly outpaces reflection and uses self-justifying arguments as dramatic action. Episodes at the gaming table make chance feel like destiny to a mind seeking patterns. The novel’s compressed social exchanges reveal how humiliation and dependency can distort what the speaker calls love or freedom.
profiles.context: Dostoevsky’s real experience of gambling is relevant, but the fictional narrator is not simply an autobiography. English spellings of names, the balance of formal and colloquial dialogue and the word choice around compulsion can vary across translators. For a close comparison, set a Kentish page beside another verified English edition, marking where the emotional rhythm changes.

themes.label: The illusion of control
themes.discussion: Gambling turns random outcomes into stories of personal mastery.

themes.label: Dependence
themes.discussion: The narrator confuses social recognition with freedom.

themes.label: Narrative self-deception
themes.discussion: Explaining a weakness can become another way to preserve it.

profiles.personal_fit: Well suited to a Dostoevsky-focused year: compact, intense, psychologically contradictory and rewarding to reread.
profiles.possible_mismatch: Repetitive gambling scenes and a deliberately frustrating narrator may not suit someone looking for stable moral guidance.

notes: Compulsive gambling and financial devastation, humiliation, emotional manipulation and volatile relationships.

series.name: Standalone
series.sequence_status: Informational connections only. All ordinary books can be manually shuffled or reordered by the reader.

profiles.summary: John Truby presents a design method for creating stories through their underlying moral and psychological relationships rather than beginning with a rigid three-act outline. His account emphasizes the interplay of a character’s weakness, desire, opponents and meaningful change as an integrated system of dramatic action.
profiles.author_and_work_background: The Anatomy of Story: 22 Steps to Becoming a Master Storyteller was first published by Farrar, Straus and Giroux in 2007, with some modern paperback catalog records showing 2008 release dates. Macmillan identifies Truby’s professional screenwriting background and the book’s philosophical and mythic examples. The twenty-two steps are professional craft advice, not experimentally proven laws of reader response.
profiles.before_reading: Use one existing novel or film as a case study and trace the protagonist’s desire, opponent and moral problem. Avoid forcing every example into one-to-one correspondence with the model. Check where the method explains a strong scene, where it proposes a useful rewrite and where it fails to account for a favorite narrative technique.
profiles.literary_approach: Truby’s premise is systemic: character, desire, opposition and plot are not detachable components but mutually formative relationships. His analytical categories can deepen revision, especially in complex ensembles. Their limitations are clearest when a text values contradiction, fragmentation or lyric reflection over conventional dramatic transformation.
profiles.context: Publisher material describes the book’s development from Truby’s teaching and screen consulting. A library record identifies a 2008 Farrar Straus and Giroux edition, explaining why listings may differ in year and pagination. Comparison with Cron and Corbett highlights three distinct practical vocabularies, not settled evidence that one model is best.

themes.label: Integrated design
themes.discussion: A narrative decision reverberates through the plot and supporting characters.

themes.label: Moral argument
themes.discussion: The conflict invites the reader to evaluate competing visions of a good life.

themes.label: Blueprint flexibility
themes.discussion: Formal structure is useful as inquiry but weak as an absolute rule.

profiles.personal_fit: Excellent for a writer managing many intersecting character arcs, a planned long novel and intricate revisions.
profiles.possible_mismatch: The detailed taxonomy may become mechanical when imposed on experimental fiction or used instead of observation.

notes: Craft examples may discuss violent, sexual or psychologically intense films; examples differ among editions.

reading_questions: What is the difference between a character’s desired outcome and their moral need?
Where does an opponent reveal a flaw the protagonist cannot see?
Can a narratively satisfying work refuse moral transformation?
Which of the twenty-two steps seems least portable across genres?
discussion_questions: How would you diagnose a scene with Truby versus Cron?
What would falsify the claim that this is the best story framework?
